data.gender_notes: Layak is used as a male name in Hindu naming traditions.
data.long_meaning: Derived from the Sanskrit word ‘Laya’, which means to lay or place. Layak is a name for a warrior or protector. The name Layak carries the meaning “Warrior” and is chosen by families in Hindu traditions for the positive qualities it expresses. Linguistically it belongs to the Sanskrit tradition and is also used in Hindi, Sanskrit, Marathi. Parents who choose Layak usually hope their child will grow to embody warrior and live with faith, good character and purpose.
data.etymology: Layak belongs to the Sanskrit linguistic tradition and is used in Hindu naming. Its recorded meaning is “Warrior.”
data.numerology_meaning: In Pythagorean numerology the letters of Layak total 5, giving a life-path number of 5. Number 5 is linked with Mercury and with the qualities of freedom, adaptability and curiosity.

data.spiritual_symbolism: Layak, in Hinduism, is a name derived from the Sanskrit word "Laya," meaning "absorption" or "attachment." As such, a Layak is one who is deeply engrossed in spiritual practices, seeking to absorb the divine essence within. This name symbolizes a strong connection to the spiritual path and a deep commitment to self-realization.

historical_references.reference: According to the Puranas, Layak is an asura or demon who was born to King Vibhishana of Lanka and his wife Tilottama. Layak is also known as Vibhishana's son Maricha. He is mentioned as a powerful asura who was a constant threat to the devas (gods).

Another reference to Layak can be found in the epic Mahabharata. In this context, Layak is mentioned as one of the four kings of the Yaksha realm, along with Kubera, Vaisravaana, and Rama. The Yakshas were nature spirits believed to bring prosperity to humans and were often depicted as guardians of treasures.

It is frequently featured on social media platforms where parents share their naming journeys, and Hindu name websites where expectant parents research meaningful names. The name bridges traditional Hindu values with modern Indian identity, making it relevant for contemporary families seeking names with deep spiritual and cultural significance.
